transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-22 15:00 PT
Duration: ~45m
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Li (Redwood SE), Laura Chen (CTO - Spectra Health), Dr. Amir Khan (AI Lead), Sam Ortiz (SRE)

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, can you hear me ok?
[00:03] Laura: yes loud and clear, thanks Maya.
[00:06] Maya: great quick agenda — a 20 minute walkthrough of the Hosted API for chat and text generation, show streaming, params, and then Ethan will dive into retries and a tiny latency note, and then Q&A.
[00:18] Dr. Khan: sounds good, our main use case is clinical note summarization, low latency is a must, also SOC 2 and patient data residency questions.
[00:27] Maya: totally understood, we'll touch on compliance and KMS, and the hosted option does have SOC 2 plus options for private deployment if needed.
[00:35] Ethan: hi all quick intro — I'm Ethan I'm the SE, I'll demo streaming and show some sample payloads, also talk about repeatable retries and idempotency keys.
[00:44] Sam: hi, Sam from infra, we mainly want to understand rate limits and how retries behave under transient errors.

--- Demo start ---
[01:10] Maya: ok pulling up the demo, this is the Redwood Console — sometimes the auto-transcript writes Redword Console so apologies if that pops up in notes, but you can see the API keys area, model catalog, and a playground for streaming.
[01:25] Maya: first, streaming. we'll send a chat completion request with stream=true and you'll get token chunks back — this helps with time-to-first-token.
[01:36] Ethan: right so instead of waiting for the full response, the client can render partial tokens. typical pattern: set stream=true, then handle tokens, and fallback to non-stream if client can't handle chunking.
[01:50] Laura: does streaming affect cost?
[01:53] Ethan: cost is per output token, streaming doesn't change billed tokens, it's purely delivery. it can reduce perceived latency for users though.

[02:05] Maya: next parameter overview — temperature, top_p, and max_tokens. default temp is 0.2 for deterministic-ish clinical outputs, you can bump to 0.7 for more creative outputs but for clinical summarization we recommend <=0.3.
[02:22] Dr. Khan: curious about top_p vs temperature — which do you recommend for safety?
[02:27] Ethan: use temperature for sampling randomness, top_p for nucleus sampling; for safety we often combine them and keep both low. also use system prompts and filters for hallucination reduction.

[03:00] Maya: quick demo of request body — we show messages array, model field, stream flag, and a client-supplied idempotency key for safe retries.
[03:12] Maya: note on max_tokens — you should set it to a reasonable cap to avoid runaway outputs and unexpected costs.

[04:00] Ethan: retries: we recommend exponential backoff and idempotency keys for POST-like generate calls. Redwood hosted will return 5xx or 429; if 5xx it's usually transient. for 429 we also recommend backoff and consider sending requests to a lower-priority model if you have throughput constraints.
[04:24] Sam: on 429s, do you expose a retry-after header?
[04:27] Ethan: yes we include Retry-After when available and also model-level throttling hints; clients should respect Retry-After.

[05:00] Maya: there's also built-in streaming reconnect behaviour in our SDKs — if a connection drops mid-stream the SDK can resume from the last token with the convo context, but that requires the client to keep track of partial offsets.
[05:14] Laura: is there a websocket option or only chunked HTTP?
[05:18] Ethan: primarily chunked HTTP/HTTP2 streaming today; websockets are on the roadmap for certain SDKs.

[06:00] Maya: demo: live request — I'm going to run a simple clinical summarization prompt with stream on.
[06:12] [stream tokens start] Ethan: (simulated token outputs) "Patient aged 67 presented with chest pain..." — you can see tokens arrive incrementally in the playground.
[06:30] Dr. Khan: that first token latency looks great, what's typical ttf?
[06:34] Ethan: depends on model & region — for our smaller open models ttf can be ~50-150ms, for larger ones 200-400ms. in hosted we publish model perf profiles in the catalog.

[07:00] Maya: caching — we support prefix caching and KV cache on the serving side which can cut token compute when prompts share prefixes; sometimes transcripts show this as "KV cache" or "K-V cash" depending on ASR.
[07:15] Laura: how does prefix caching affect correctness?
[07:18] Ethan: it's transparent, only reuses computed KV cache for identical prefixes; if context changes you won't hit the cache. it reduces cost and latency for repeated prompts.

[08:00] Maya: security/compliance — hosted API supports SOC 2, SAML SSO, RBAC, audit logs and KMS for encryption at rest. for PHI workloads we typically recommend private deployment but a lot of customers run with hosted + strict DLP and limited retention.
[08:20] Dr. Khan: we need data residency in US East only, is that supported?
[08:24] Maya: yes, region pinning is available and we can restrict to specific regions; we'll include that in the security pack.

[09:00] Sam: what about logs — who can see the logs and how long are they retained?
[09:05] Maya: audit logs are tenant-scoped, retention configurable as an add-on. we can push logs to your SIEM and support ingest via secure connectors.

[10:00] Ethan: quick note on failure modes — transient GPU OOMs can cause 5xx; in hosted we have autoscaling and fallback models so customers rarely see hard failures. fallback can route to a quantized variant which trades off latency/cost.
[10:20] Laura: quantized variant — less accuracy?
[10:23] Ethan: slightly lower quality on edge cases; we surface quality regression metrics so you can set a rollout policy.

[12:00] Maya: pricing overview at a high level — per-token billing for hosted, and reserved capacity for Dedicated if you need throughput guarantees.
[12:12] Dr. Khan: roughly what's the unit cost difference between hosted and dedicated?
[12:16] Maya: dedicated is lower per-token at committed volumes but requires a commit; we shared a pricing doc in the deck, I'll resend.

[14:00] Laura: are there example SDKs for streaming in Python and JS?
[14:03] Ethan: yes both, and we have sample code for reconnect + idempotency. I'll drop the links.

[16:00] Maya: switching to a short live benchmark slide — we're happy to run a 1-hour latency bench with your sample prompts; Ethan will provide a script that you can run on-prem to compare or we can run from our hosted infra.
[16:18] Ethan: the script will measure time-to-first-token, median token latency, and P95 for a sequence length of 512 tokens.

[18:00] Dr. Khan: perfect, that'll help us evaluate. also we may run a PoC to test PHI handling — any blockers?
[18:10] Maya: only that we need to align on retention and region; otherwise PoC is straightforward.

[20:00] Q&A and small clarifs:
[20:05] Sam: any SLOs for ttf?
[20:08] Ethan: we publish model-level SLOs for hosted, and for Dedicated you can get contract SLOs.
[21:00] Laura: what's the onboarding time?
[21:05] Maya: self-serve in minutes for basic keys; for enterprise security review + SOC2 it's typically 2-4 weeks.

--- Wrap up / Next steps ---
[43:00] Maya: quick recap: we'll send SOC2 + security pack, Ethan will share the benchmark script and sample prompts, and schedule a POC scoping call next week.
[43:20] Laura: sounds good, thanks everyone.
[43:25] Dr. Khan: thanks, appreciate the clarity.
[43:30] Maya: thank you all -- I'll follow up with notes and the docs.

[End of transcript]
